content: The Emergency Alert System (EAS) was established in 1994, replacing the Emergency Broadcast System (EBS). It is managed collaboratively by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and the National Weather Service (NWS). The primary purpose of the EAS is to allow the President of the United States to address the nation within 10 minutes during a national emergency, although this capability has never been utilized. The regulations and standards governing the EAS are overseen by the FCC's Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau. Each state and several U.S. territories have their own EAS plans. The EAS encompasses a wide range of communication platforms, including AM/FM radio, television (VHF and UHF), cable television, satellite radio, and digital broadcasting systems. Since December 31, 2006, digital television, digital cable, and satellite radio providers have been required to participate in the EAS. Direct broadcast satellite providers, such as DIRECTV and Dish Network, have been required to comply since May 31, 2007. Video Dial Tone (OVS) systems have been included since July 1, 2007. EAS messages consist of four components: a digitally encoded SAME (Specific Area Message Encoding) header, an attention signal, an audio announcement, and a digitally encoded end-of-message marker. The SAME header contains critical information, such as the origin of the alert (e.g., the President, state or local authorities, the NWS, or broadcasters), a brief description of the event (e.g., tornado, flood), the affected areas (up to 32 counties or states), the expected duration of the event, the date and time of issuance (in UTC), and the identification of the originating station. To ensure redundancy, the SAME header is repeated three times, as it lacks error detection codes. EAS decoders compare the received headers to ensure accuracy and determine whether to relay the message based on its relevance to the local area. The attention signal used in the EAS varies depending on the platform. On NOAA Weather Radio stations, it is a specific tone, while on commercial broadcast stations, it is a two-tone combination of 853 Hz and 960 Hz sine waves, similar to the signal used in the older EBS. This two-tone system is no longer mandatory as of 1998 but may still be used for audio alerts preceding EAS messages. Following the attention signal, a voice message provides details about the alert. The message concludes with three bursts of the AFSK End of Message (EOM) signal. The White House has endorsed the transition to the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP), and FEMA is actively testing its implementation. CAP is expected to enhance the system's capabilities and allow state governors to mandate universal activation of the EAS within their states. The FCC requires all broadcast stations to install and maintain EAS decoders and encoders at their control points. These devices continuously monitor signals from nearby stations for EAS messages. Stations must monitor at least two other source stations, one of which must be a designated local primary. Stations are also required to retain the latest version of the EAS handbook and maintain detailed logs of all received and transmitted EAS messages. These logs can be kept manually or electronically, provided they are accessible for review. Television stations must transmit both audio and visual messages during EAS activations. Visual messages are typically displayed as a text crawl at the top of the screen, often color-coded to indicate the priority of the alert. Some stations may only transmit the visual message, which is outside the requirements. However, audio is necessary if the station is used for monitoring by another station. EAS equipment must be tested weekly. The Required Weekly Test (RWT) includes the SAME header and end-of-message bursts but does not require an audio message. Television stations are not obligated to transmit a video message for weekly tests. Required Monthly Tests (RMTs) are more comprehensive and involve suspending normal programming to broadcast a coordinated test message. RMTs must be conducted during specific timeframes and retransmitted within 60 minutes of receipt. The EAS has expanded to include 80 event types, initially focused on weather-related emergencies but now encompassing non-weather emergencies, such as AMBER Alerts for child abductions. The FCC has sought public input on improving the EAS and has provisionally endorsed replacing the SAME protocol with CAP. The EAS is designed to serve the entire public, not just those with SAME-capable equipment. Consumer-level radios, particularly weather radios, are widely available and often pre-tuned to stations providing emergency alerts. These radios can narrow alerts to specific areas, reducing false warnings and ensuring that only those in danger are notified. The National Weather Service advocates for every home to have both a smoke detector and a SAME weather radio. New infrastructure, such as the Digital Emergency Alert System, is under development to transmit alerts directly to citizens and responders via computers, mobile phones, and other devices without requiring specialized receivers. The EAS has faced challenges and incidents, such as accidental activations. For example, on February 1, 2005, an erroneous EAS message in Connecticut instructed residents to evacuate the state. On June 26, 2007, an accidental Emergency Action Notification (EAN) activation in Illinois caused widespread disruption. These incidents highlight the importance of rigorous testing and oversight. The EAS is widely recognized and has been referenced in popular culture, including television shows and music. For instance, an episode of Dexter's Laboratory humorously depicted an EAS test interrupting the protagonist's favorite show.
